additional_requirements: Functioning is not markedly impaired apart from the impact of the delusion(s) or its ramifications

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

symptom.disease_info: Delusional disorder is characterized by the presence of one or more persistent, non-bizarre or minimally bizarre delusions lasting at least one month in a person whose overall functioning is relatively preserved and whose behavior is not obviously odd or markedly disorganized outside the delusional context. Aside from the delusional beliefs, mood and thought processes are often relatively intact, and criteria for schizophrenia (such as prominent hallucinations, disorganized speech, or negative symptoms) are not met. Onset is typically in mid to late adulthood and may be associated with psychosocial stressors, social isolation, sensory impairment, or personality traits such as suspiciousness or rigidity. The course is usually chronic, with beliefs that remain fixed despite clear contradictory evidence, and individuals may only come to clinical attention when interpersonal conflict, legal problems, or functional decline arise directly from their delusional convictions.

patient.personality: Malcolm is an outgoing, creative, and community-oriented designer who thrives on collaboration and social energy but often overcommits to projects and nightlife at the expense of rest.
patient.stressor: About a year ago, Malcolm hit a rough patch when a major branding contract he’d invested months of work into was abruptly canceled after internal changes at the client company, followed closely by critical online feedback on one of his public design installations. Proud of his self-taught trajectory and sensitive to professional respect, he began to brood over the cancellations and comments, combing through design forums and social media, and gradually came to feel that specific industry peers were taking ideas from him and subtly undermining his reputation. Over the ensuing months, he became more guarded in workshops, less willing to share drafts, and increasingly focused on tracing supposed patterns in others’ portfolios and posts that he believed confirmed a particular, unshakeable explanation for his stalled opportunities. When collaborators started distancing themselves, citing how hard it had become to discuss feedback with him, and a close friend pointed out how much his work decisions were being driven by these fixed assumptions, Malcolm agreed—reluctantly—to seek psychiatric help to sort out why he couldn’t let go of these beliefs despite how much conflict they were causing.
patient.chief_complaint: “I’m stuck on these beliefs about what people in my field are doing to my work, and even when everyone tells me I’m wrong, I just can’t see it any other way.”

S019.manifestation: No matter how many times people tell me it’s a coincidence, I’m convinced a few specific designers in the scene are watching my socials, lifting my concepts, and quietly warning others not to work with me, because I keep seeing my ideas show up in their portfolios and little digs about my style buried in their posts and comments.
